story_title: The Mitten with the Small Stars
summary: Ines Larkspur closes the tea room, feeds the coal stove and knits one patterned mitten for the ferry pilot, a band of stars and then pine sprigs. The stove burns low, the cat sleeps on the warm tiles, and Ines dozes with the wool on her knee.
source_tradition: Baltic folk knitting (patterned mittens with star and pine bands), Latvia and neighbouring coast
source_note: Traditional hand-knitting patterns are a folk craft in the public domain; the story, characters and wording are entirely original.

description_summary: A slow evening of knitting at a small seaside tea room, told gently over a crackling coal stove, with stove sounds after the story to stay asleep.
description_setting: Mid October in Fernwick. The Green Kettle has closed for the night, the stove is low and warm, and Ines Larkspur knits a patterned mitten for the ferry pilot while the cat sleeps on the tiles.
image_brief: A seaside tea room at night seen through a large warm amber window, a cat curled on the tiles and a chair beside a glowing coal stove, a little frost at the corners of the glass. Deep navy and teal shadows, one warm light source, no faces, no religious symbols.

new_world_facts: Ines keeps her knitting in an old basket whose lid never quite shuts.
A worn pattern card with bands of stars and pine sprigs came from a biscuit tin and is folded in four.
Ines is knitting a pair of mittens for Barnaby Teague; the first mitten is finished and the second begins tomorrow.
The clock over the counter at the Green Kettle always seems to say quarter to nine.
The lamplighter rides a bicycle along Harbor Lane.
script:
Welcome back to Fernwick.

[pause]

It is the middle of October, and the evening has turned cool and dry. The leaves on the green have gone the color of toast, and a little smoke from someone's chimney hangs over the lane. At the Green Kettle, the tea room with six tables and a coal stove, the last customer has left and the sign in the door has been turned to Closed.

[pause]

Ines Larkspur does what she does every night at this hour. She carries the cups back to the shelf and sets them in a row. Then she moves the third cup to the front, looks at it, and puts it back where it was. The six cups are exactly as they were this morning, and she is satisfied.

[pause]

She opens the little iron door of the stove and looks in. The coal has burned down to a bed of orange, with a thin blue flame walking along the top. She lifts the scuttle, slides in three lumps, and closes the door with her foot. The stove ticks twice, as it always does, and then settles into a low, steady mutter.

[pause]

The window beside the stove is fogged at the corners. Beyond it, Harbor Lane is empty, and the lamps along the water make small yellow pools on the stones. Inside, the room is the warmest it has been all day. The tables are wiped, the floor is swept, and nothing is left to do.

[long pause]

So Ines fetches her knitting basket from beneath the counter. It is an old basket, with a lid that never quite shuts. Inside are two balls of wool, one the gray of wet slate and one the cream of fresh milk, and a set of five thin needles with a half-finished mitten hanging from them.

[pause]

The mitten is for Barnaby Teague, who pilots the ferry to Wren Island. Barnaby counts waves in a murmur all the way across the water, and he does it with bare hands on the wheel. Ines has noticed that his knuckles turn pink by the second week of October. She decided about a month ago that this was a problem a pair of mittens could solve.

[pause]

She carries the basket to the chair beside the stove, the one with the cushion that has taken the shape of her. She sits, and the chair lets out a small creak of welcome. She tucks a cup of tea on the arm of the chair, though the tea went lukewarm an hour ago, and she picks up the needles.

[pause]

The pattern comes from a worn card she found in a biscuit tin. The card was folded in four and soft as cloth, and it showed a band of tiny stars, then a band of pine sprigs, then stars again. It is a very old way of making mittens, from a country on the far side of the sea, where the winters are long and every family had its own patterns. Nobody in Fernwick has ever heard of it, which is part of why she likes it.

[pause]

She knits one row of cream, then one of gray. The wool passes over her finger and under, over and under, and the two colors twist together at the back where no one will see. There is a rhythm to it. Over, under. Over, under. The needles click, and the stove ticks, and the sounds begin to keep time with one another.

[pause]

Halfway up the hand, the first star appears. It is a small cream diamond on a gray field, no bigger than a lentil. Ines turns the mitten to look at it and nods. Then she starts the second star beside it, and the third, until a little row of them sits across the back of the hand like lamps along a lane.

[long pause]

Somewhere in the middle of the stars, Ines begins to hum. It is no particular tune, just a few low notes that wander up and down and end up where they started. She has hummed it for so many winters that she no longer notices. The stove seems to like it, and the coal glows a little brighter on each long note.

[pause]

Pip comes in from the back room. Nobody has ever been sure whose cat Pip is, but tonight Pip belongs to the Green Kettle. The cat walks the length of the room without hurry, inspects the warm tiles in front of the stove, and lowers herself onto them in a slow, round heap. One ear turns toward the knitting. Then the ear turns back.

[pause]

The stove mutters on. A lump of coal shifts and falls, and a little shower of orange sparks drifts up and fades. Ines does not look up. Her hands know where they are going. Cream, gray, cream. The stars are done, and now the pine sprigs begin, each one a little green-gray feather of stitches leaning to the left.

[pause]

On the shelf behind her, the six cups catch the stove light, each one holding a small orange flame in its curve. A teaspoon rests in the saucer of the fourth. It has rested there since closing, and no one has disturbed it. The whole room has the look of a place that has finished its day and is quietly pleased about it.

[pause]

Outside, the lamplighter's bicycle ticks past the window. The sound is far away, and it fades. The glass has fogged a little more, and the lane has gone soft and blurry, like a picture seen through steam. Inside, the clock over the counter has been saying quarter to nine for some time now. It is a very patient clock.

[pause]

Ines reaches the top of the hand. She counts the stitches softly to herself and finds the number she wanted. She begins to narrow the top, a few stitches at a time, so the mitten will close over the fingers like a small, round roof. The rows are shorter now, and they go faster.

[long pause]

Her eyes feel heavy, and she lets them. The needles keep on for a few more rows, slower and slower. Over, under. Over, under. The wool is warm in her hands. The cream is almost the color of the stove light, and the gray is almost the color of the shadows, and the two together make something very like the evening.

[pause]

The last row is finished. She draws the wool through the final loops and pulls it snug. She holds the mitten up to the lamp, and the stars and pine sprigs stand out clearly. It is only one mitten, and the other will be started tomorrow, but one is a good beginning.

[long pause]

She sets it on her knee. She means to find the pair needle and begin the second, but the chair is warm, and the stove is low, and there is no hurry in the room at all. Her hand rests on the soft wool. The tea sits cold and forgotten on the arm of the chair.

[long pause]

Pip stretches out one paw toward the stove and sighs. The coal settles. The clock says quarter to nine. The mitten lies on Ines's knee with its small stars facing up, and her shoulders have settled low and loose.

[long pause]

The lamps along Harbor Lane burn on, one after another, all the way to the water. In the Green Kettle, six cups wait on their shelf in a row.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[pause]

The Green Kettle is closed. The cups are in their row. The stove is low and warm.

[pause]

Ines sits by the stove with her knitting. She is making a mitten for Barnaby. It has gray wool and cream wool, and a band of small stars.

[pause]

Over, under. Over, under. The needles click. The stove ticks.

[long pause]

The stars are done. Now come the pine sprigs. Cream, gray, cream.

[pause]

Pip lies on the warm tiles. The coal settles. The clock says quarter to nine.

[long pause]

The mitten is finished. Ines lays it on her knee. Her hand rests on the wool. Her eyes close.

[long pause]

The stove is low. The room is warm. The lamps are low in Fernwick.

[long pause]

Good night.
